title: Fitting a kitchen monoblock tap
subtitle: Remove an old kitchen tap and fit a single-hole monobloc mixer tap using flexible tap connectors and a basin wrench
excerpt: How to fit a kitchen monobloc mixer tap into a single-hole sink. Covers isolating the supply, removing the old tap, fitting the new monobloc with back-nut and flexible hose connectors, and testing for leaks.
sourceNotes: Collins Complete DIY Manual (referenced, not reproduced). Reader's Digest Complete DIY Manual (referenced, not reproduced). UK Water Regulations Advisory Scheme guidance on tap fitting (open access).

glossaryTerms.definition: A single-body mixer tap fitted through one hole in the sink or worktop. Hot and cold supplies connect to the two tails at the bottom of the body; a single spout and lever (or pair of levers) mixes the water. The single-hole format is the standard for modern kitchen sinks.

A short braided stainless steel hose (150 to 600 mm) with a compression fitting at one end and a threaded nut at the other, used to connect a tap tail to the supply pipe. Flexible connectors allow minor misalignment between the tap tails and the supply pipes. Available in 15 mm compression to 3/8 inch BSP and other common sizes.

Isolate the supply and drain the section

Close the local service valves under the sink if there are any. If not, close the main stopcock. Open the tap to run off the water in the supply pipes. Have a bowl and a thick towel ready under the work position.

Disconnect the supply pipes from the tap tails; either unscrew the compression nuts or the flexible connector nuts. Use the basin wrench to undo the back nut underneath the sink. The back nut is the only fixing holding the tap body; once it is off, the tap lifts free. Clean off any old sealing compound or washer debris from the sink surface.

Check the sink hole diameter matches the tap body. Fit the rubber or plastic gasket to the base of the tap where it contacts the sink surface. Thread the tap through the hole from above. Under the sink, fit the plastic top-hat washer and the back nut onto the tap tail threads. Tighten the back nut with the basin wrench until the tap body is firm and cannot rotate. Do not overtighten: the ceramic or stainless sink can crack under point loading.

Connect the flexible tap connectors between the tap tails and the supply pipes. Wrap the male threaded connector ends with three or four turns of PTFE tape before screwing into the supply isolation valve or the supply pipe fitting. Tighten by hand then a quarter-turn with the spanner. Open the isolation valves slowly and check for drips at each connection. Drips at a compression fitting: tighten the compression nut a quarter-turn. Drips at a threaded joint: drain, add more PTFE tape, and reconnect.

attrs.symptom: Tap body rotates when the lever is operated
attrs.fix: Tighten the back nut with the basin wrench while holding the tap body still from above.

attrs.symptom: Water pressure is poor from the new tap compared to the old
attrs.cause: The flexible connectors are kinked, or the in-tap flow limiters (fitted in some taps) are installed in a supply that has low pressure.
attrs.fix: Check that the flexible connectors are not kinked under the sink. Check for built-in flow limiters in the tap tails and remove them if the supply pressure is low.
